Bramwell Ashdown.narrative: I am Master woodcutter at the Ferncross, and the oak and ash of this crossing have paid my house's way for twenty years. I fell for Elmwick and Reedmoor both, and keep the charcoal pits on the side when the burn runs slow and the orders run fast. I owe Alder Rush a share of charcoal from last winter's burn and have not carried it up the road yet; the Elmwick timber paid marks in hand, and Alder can wait a little longer without the world ending. I count Orvin Hollis at Sootwood a friend, and I have not forgotten the men from Coldwell who walked off with my tools.
values: a fair price for honest work
the crossing fed before anyone else
debts paid, though not always first
keeping my word to my neighbours
goals: carry Alder Rush his charcoal share before he has to ask twice
keep the Ferncross timber trade with both Elmwick and Reedmoor
see my daughter Corliss learn the axe and the pits without hurting herself
get back the tools the Coldwell men took
make a hafted axe myself, from felling to finished, that Corliss can swing true
take Nesta down the stone road to Kettlebridge on a carters' day, just to see the clock tower
Bramwell Ashdown.mood: steady, a little pressed, keeping his worries behind his teeth

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She keeps the pot and the tally both; I would be lost at the crossing without her.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Quick with kindling and quicker with questions; I want her to have the axe and the sense to use it.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: He lent grain last winter and I owe him charcoal; he is patient but he counts.

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: fellow woodcutter
relations.note: She sold Elmwick timber for the Lakemead fence and says a sale is a sale; I say it is, but Reedmoor may not.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His barley came in light and the kitchen needs it; I would rather buy than beg.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She buys our timber and now she is cool with the crossing over a fence; I want that to blow over.

relations.name: Hob Garrow
relations.label: customer
relations.note: Elmwick pays on time and asks few questions; I would not want to lose his orders.

relations.name: Orvin Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: A good man with an axe and a bad word for the quay's stone price; we understand each other.

relations.name: Marta Hale
relations.label: grudge
relations.note: Her people took my tools off the wood road; I have not had a good word for Coldwell since.

relations.name: Sorrel Bramblecap
relations.label: trade neighbour
relations.note: He works the hollow's grain and berry rows and grumbles about the giants' track taking timber; I sell him nothing and buy nothing, but the east road keeps us honest with each other.

memories.gist: The Lean Year came and the berry crop failed; I felled and burned all through it and still the crossing went hungry, and Alder Rush's grain kept us.
Two men from Coldwell stopped me on the wood road and took my tools and a load of charcoal; I walked home with empty hands.
Corliss stacked her first charcoal pit with me and never once let the fire go out.
Odelia Harrow sold a load of Elmwick timber for the Lakemead fence, and Nell Sedge heard of it and came down cold on the crossing.
I sat with Orvin Hollis at the Ferncross market and we agreed the seawall will never be built and the quay will pay dear for it.

stances.why: A man who owes and does not pay cannot ask for credit when the burn goes bad.
Nesta's pot feeds the woodcutters; whatever the orders, the crossing eats before the marks go out.
Odelia Harrow sold Elmwick timber and that was her trade to make; I will not call it treason.
Nell Sedge buys our timber and Reedmoor's fish comes up the road; a fence quarrel must not cost us that.
They took my tools on the wood road and I have not seen them since.

Bramwell Ashdown.secret: The Elmwick order came first because it paid marks in hand, and I told Alder Rush the pits burned slow. I would not say that to his face.
pastimes: sitting by the charcoal pit through the night with a flask and a story
walking the crossing at first light to read which way the wind will take the burn
a cup at the Sootwood with Orvin Hollis when a load takes him that way
Bramwell Ashdown.calling: Give me oak and ash and a clean-burning pit, and I'll feed my house and half the crossing besides.

Nesta Ashdown.narrative: I keep the Ferncross kitchen and the common pot, and there are more woodcutters at my table this winter than the plot can carry. Roderick Harrow's barley came in light and I am feeding his men as well as my own, so I am watching the store and the weather both. I trade bread and broth for fish and fibre, and I would rather owe a neighbour a kindness than see a man go hungry at my fire. The crossing holds together because somebody keeps the pot on.
values: nobody goes hungry at the crossing
a fair trade for bread and broth
goals: get Roderick Harrow to sell me barley on credit before the store runs out
keep the woodcutters fed through the winter
trade bread for fish with Tansy Sedge and Thistle Mossfoot when their packs come
see Corliss safe and warm through the cold
have a proper larder of my own again, salted and full by first frost
see Corliss keep a kitchen of her own one day, and teach her the pot before she goes
Nesta Ashdown.mood: worried and busy, with a calm face for the table

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He fells and I feed; he worries at the debts and I worry at the pot, and between us it works.

relations.name: Corliss Ashdown
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She stacks kindling and asks about the quay; I want her to see it one day, and to come home.

relations.name: Roderick Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: His barley came in light and I need it on credit; I hope he sees the kitchen is feeding his men too.

relations.name: Odelia Harrow
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She works the south side and keeps the tally; we share what the two houses have and watch the sky.

relations.name: Maren Hollis
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We met at the Ferncross market and have traded ever since; she knows what a thin store means.

relations.name: Tansy Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her bread and my broth go back and forth along the east road; she is fair with the fish.

relations.name: Thistle Mossfoot
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His packs bring fish and fibre and take my bread; a small folk pedlar who pays what he says.

relations.name: Alder Rush
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: Bramwell owes him charcoal and he has not pressed us; I do not forget that.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: customer
relations.note: She buys timber and now she is cool with the crossing; I would rather mend it over a bowl than argue.

relations.name: Mallow Bramblecap
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: She feeds a hollow's common table and I feed a crossing's, so she knows what a thin store means; her people's bread and honey come up the path to me when there is any to spare.

memories.gist: The Lean Year: I stretched the pot with roots and nettles and fed the woodcutters through, and I have never let the store get that low again without counting it.
Corliss was small and burned her hand on the pot hook; I salved it and she has been careful at the fire since.
Maren Hollis came down the wood road with roots and charcoal and we traded half a day's bread for it at the Ferncross market.
Roderick Harrow told me his barley came in light, and I looked at my store and knew we would be sharing thin bread before the thaw.

stances.why: The common pot is the crossing's hearth; a woodcutter who eats here works here, and no one is turned away hungry.
Roderick's barley is in his barn and my store is thin; a neighbour's credit is cheaper than a hungry winter.
The plot will not carry more woodcutters than it has before, and the cold comes early down the wood road.
Fish and fibre come up the east road and my bread goes down it; that trade keeps the pot from being only roots.
Reedmoor and Elmwick can quarrel over a meadow; I will not have it at my table when both bring fish.

Nesta Ashdown.secret: I have been putting a little less in each bowl so the store lasts longer, and I have not told Bramwell how thin it truly is.
pastimes: baking a week's bread on the crossing's one good oven day
swapping news and recipes with Maren Hollis over a mending basket
walking the wood edge at dusk to see what the small folk's packs have brought
Nesta Ashdown.calling: Anyone who sits at my table eats; that is the whole of my work and I am proud of it.

Corliss Ashdown.narrative: I stack the kindling and learn the axe and the charcoal burn beside my father, and I am quicker at the stacks than he thinks. When the Fernhollow folk come up the path I play with Fennel Underbank, and I want more than anything to see the quay at Lanternquay and the boats. The wolves come down the wood road in winter and I do not like the sound of them at night.
values: learning the axe and the burn
goals: learn to stack a pit that does not smoke
see the quay at Lanternquay one day
keep the wolves away from the kindling stacks
learn to sharpen the axe without nicking the blade
get a look at a real boat, even a little one, before the year is out
Corliss Ashdown.mood: curious and restless, brave by day and fearful at night

relations.name: Bramwell Ashdown
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me stack the kindling and says I am quicker than he was; I want him to teach me the axe proper.

relations.name: Nesta Ashdown
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She keeps the pot and never lets me go cold; she says the quay is a long way and I say it is not so far.

relations.name: Fennel Underbank
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He comes up the path with the Fernhollow folk and we play among the stacks; he knows every flower.

relations.name: Tamsin Harrow
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She helps with the goats and the garden and we play at the crossing when the work is done.

relations.name: Tace Hollis
relations.label: stranger
relations.note: She stacks pits at Sootwood and knows a quay knot; I want to learn it.

memories.gist: I stacked my first charcoal pit with my father and never once let the fire go out, and he said I had the hand for it.
I burned my hand on the pot hook when I was small and my mother salved it; I have been careful at the fire since.
Wolves came down the wood road in the night and I heard them from my bed; I do not go far from the stacks after dark.

stances.why: My father says the pits are the crossing's living and I want to be good at them.
The quay folk come up the wood road with fish and talk of boats; I want to see it with my own eyes.
The wolves come down the wood road and I have heard them.

pastimes: stacking kindling into little towers and knocking them down
playing hide-and-seek in the undergrowth with Fennel Underbank
watching the charcoal pit glow and feeding it a stick at a time
Corliss Ashdown.calling: I want to be a woodcutter like Father, but quicker, and maybe with a boat as well.
